c.tagline: Walled Caribbean jewel of colonial plazas, salsa and golden light.

taxi.fareNote: Street taxis are unmetered and run on fixed zone fares — agree the price before getting in, especially from the airport. Uber operates in a legal grey area, while inDrive and Cabify are widely used to book a tracked ride.

emergency.note: 123 is Colombia's free, 24/7 unified emergency line reaching police, ambulance and fire; 125 is the ambulance line and 119 the fire department.

hood_landmark.Getsemaní: Plaza de la Trinidad, Getsemaní, Cartagena

avoid.reason: The walled city is safe; use caution around Bazurto market and in outer barrios. Drink-spiking in nightlife.

hood_desc: The UNESCO-listed walled old city of pastel colonial mansions, flowered balconies, churches and shady plazas — Cartagena's must-see core and where most first-timers stay to be steps from the sights.
A once-gritty barrio just outside the walls, now Cartagena's hippest quarter of street art, salsa bars, backpacker hostels and buzzing Plaza de la Trinidad nightlife.
A modern high-rise beach strip on a slim peninsula lined with hotels, malls and restaurants; suits travelers who want a sea-front resort base and long grey-sand beaches.
The quieter northern corner of the walled city around leafy Plaza de San Diego, full of boutique hotels, artisan shops and intimate restaurants; refined and central without Getsemaní's crowds.
A leafy residential island of early-20th-century republican mansions and marinas just south of the center; a calmer, more local base a short ride from the old city.
lodging: ESTELAR Cartagena de Indias Hotel & Centro de Convenciones

water.note: Cartagena's tap water is potable, though many visitors still choose bottled.

transit.hours: Transcaribe and city buses run roughly 5:00 AM to 11:00 PM; after that, taxis and ride apps cover late-night trips.
transit.note: Cartagena has no metro or rail. The Transcaribe BRT runs a trunk line through the city, supplemented by traditional colectivo buses; within the compact walled city, most visitors simply walk.
transit.pay: Transcaribe uses a rechargeable smartcard (tarjeta Transcaribe) bought and topped up at stations; traditional buses are paid in cash to the driver.

bus: Intercity buses from Terminal de Transporte de Cartagena
ferry: Tourist boats to Islas del Rosario & Barú (Muelle de la Bodeguita)

transit.m: Transcaribe/city bus toward the center, ~20-30 min
Fixed-fare taxi to the Walled City, ~15 min

tip.r: A 10% 'propina voluntaria' (voluntary service charge) is often added to restaurant bills; you can accept, adjust or decline it. Rounding up for taxis is not expected.

food.name: Arepa de huevo
food.desc: Fried corn patty split open, filled with a whole egg and refried until crisp. Cartagena's classic street breakfast, best eaten hot from the cart.

places.name: Mila Cafe
places.note: Colonial-house cafe doing a tidy sit-down version of the arepa e' huevo alongside its famous desserts.

places.name: Tomillo
places.note: Modern Caribbean kitchen serving arepas de huevo and other Cartagenero classics done properly.

places.name: Mercado Bazurto fry stalls
places.note: The chaotic local market where the fritos are cheapest, freshest and entirely un-touristed.

food.name: Ceviche cartagenero
food.desc: Caribbean-style ceviche of shrimp or white fish in lime with tomato, onion and often a splash of coconut milk or pink sauce.

places.name: La Cevicheria
places.note: The city's most famous ceviche house on Calle Stuart, packed since the Bourdain years and still consistent.

places.name: Tomillo
places.note: Specialises in ceviches and raw seafood with local fish and less of a queue than the walled-city names.

places.name: El Boliche Cebicheria
places.note: Tiny eight-table room turning out inventive tamarind and coconut ceviches from the day's catch.

food.name: Posta negra cartagenera
food.desc: Beef round braised for hours in a dark, sweet-savoury panela and soy sauce until it slices like butter, served with coconut rice.

places.name: La Mulata
places.note: Colourful lunch-menu institution whose posta negra is marinated two days; go early, it sells out.

places.name: Mila Cafe
places.note: Serves posta negra among its Cartagena savoury classics in an air-conditioned colonial room.

places.name: Tomillo
places.note: Does a refined posta cartagenera plus arepas and empanadas from local producers.

food.name: Cazuela de mariscos
food.desc: Rich coconut-cream seafood casserole with shrimp, squid, fish and crab, ladled over white or coconut rice with fried plantain.

places.name: La Cevicheria
places.note: Coconut-heavy cazuela using the same day-boat seafood as its ceviches.

places.name: La Mulata
places.note: Home-style cazuela on the rotating daily menu at very fair walled-city prices.

places.name: La Cocina de Pepina
places.note: Afro-Caribbean cooking from the Bolivar coast; cazuelas and stews made the way island families make them.

food.desc: Whole fried red snapper with smashed fried plantains, coconut rice and a lime-and-onion suero. The definitive Caribbean beach plate.

places.name: La Cocina de Pepina
places.note: Beloved neighbourhood kitchen for arroz de lisa, coconut rice and fried fish done without shortcuts.

places.name: Mercado Bazurto fondas
places.note: Market cookshops fry the morning's catch to order for a fraction of old-town prices.

places.name: Beach shacks at Playa Blanca
places.note: Day-trip standard: pick your snapper on the sand and eat it with patacones and coco rice.

food.name: Fritos cartageneros
food.desc: Deep-fried snack canon: carimanolas of yuca and meat, cheese-stuffed empanadas, dedos de queso and buttery pandebono.

places.name: Plaza de la Trinidad carts
places.note: Evening square where locals gather and a dozen carts fry carimanolas and arepas until late.

places.name: Mercado Bazurto fry stalls
places.note: The city's fritos heartland; go with a guide in the morning for the widest choice.

places.name: Portal de los Dulces stalls

food.name: Limonada de coco
food.desc: Cartagena's signature cooler: lime juice blended with coconut milk and ice into a frosty, faintly sweet slush. Non-alcoholic and everywhere.

places.name: La Cevicheria
places.note: Widely cited as the benchmark version, thick and properly tart.

places.name: La Mulata
places.note: Comes with the lunch menu and is a cheap way to try the real thing.

places.name: Beachfront kiosks on Bocagrande
places.note: Blended to order at seafront carts for a few thousand pesos.

food.desc: Tart, deep-magenta juice from the corozo palm fruit, drunk straight, sweetened, or spiked with rum in local cocktails.

places.name: Alquimico
places.note: Three-floor cocktail bar on Latin America's 50 Best list that champions corozo and other Colombian fruits.

places.name: Mercado Bazurto juice stalls

places.name: La Cocina de Pepina

landmarks: Ciudad Amurallada (Walled City)
Eleven kilometers of coral-stone ramparts wrap a UNESCO old town of bougainvillea-draped balconies, plazas, and pastel facades, the Caribbean's most romantic colonial ensemble.
Castillo San Felipe de Barajas
The greatest fortress the Spanish ever built in the Americas, a pyramid of tunnels and batteries that repelled pirates and admirals alike since 1657.
Torre del Reloj
The iconic yellow clock tower gate, principal entrance to the walled city since colonial times, opens onto the statue-studded Plaza de los Coches.
Getsemaní
Once gritty, now electric, this barrio of street art, fluttering flags, and salsa-filled Plaza de la Trinidad is Cartagena's most vibrant neighborhood after dark.
Catedral de Santa Catalina de Alejandría
Cartagena's 16th-century cathedral, its coral-hued dome and bell tower rising above the skyline, survived Francis Drake's cannon fire during construction.
Palacio de la Inquisición
Behind one of the city's finest baroque portals, this museum unflinchingly displays the Spanish Inquisition's torture instruments alongside Cartagena's tumultuous history.
Convento de la Popa
Crowning the city's highest hill, this 17th-century convent with a flowering courtyard delivers the definitive panorama over Cartagena, its bay, and beyond.
Las Bóvedas
Twenty-three dungeon vaults built into the ramparts, once ammunition stores and jail cells, now a colorful arcade of handicraft and emerald shops.
Plaza Santo Domingo and Botero's Gertrudis
The old town's liveliest square pairs the city's oldest church with Fernando Botero's voluptuous bronze reclining figure, polished by countless good-luck touches.
Convento e Iglesia de San Pedro Claver
A 17th-century Jesuit convent and church honoring the priest who ministered to enslaved Africans, its museum holding religious art and his glass-encased remains.

train.note: Colombia has no scheduled passenger railway serving Cartagena; the only surviving passenger trains are tourist operations near Bogota such as the Tren de la Sabana and Turistren, none of which reach the Caribbean coast.

bus.note: Every intercity coach uses the Terminal de Transportes de Cartagena on the Carretera de la Cordialidad in Barrio Pozon, a good 20 to 30 minutes east of the walled city by taxi or on the Transcaribe feeder, so allow far more time than the distance suggests. Expreso Brasilia (https://www.expresobrasilia.com/), Berlinas del Fonce, Copetran, Unitransco and Rapido Ochoa share the domestic network; typical runs are Barranquilla in about 2 hours, Santa Marta in 4 to 5, Medellin in around 13 and Bogota in roughly 20, with overnight servicio de lujo coaches on the Bogota and Bucaramanga routes. No operator sells a scheduled through-coach across a border from Cartagena: for Venezuela you travel to Maicao or Cucuta and cross on foot, and there is no road link at all to Panama because of the Darien Gap.

intl.to: San Blas Islands & Portobelo area (Panama) - shared sailing passage from Cartagena's Manga marinas

ferry.note: Day boats to the Islas del Rosario, Baru and Playa Blanca leave from the Muelle Turistico de la Bodeguita next to the walled city, generally between about 07:30 and 09:00 with returns mid-afternoon, but they are run by many small licensed lancha operators and sold at the dock or through hotels rather than by a single ferry company, with a port tax and marine park fee collected on the day. Crossings run from about 45 minutes to 1.5 hours depending on the island, and the December to February windy season brings choppy seas and cancellations. The Cartagena to Panama passage sold by Blue Sailing is a five-night shared sailing charter through the San Blas islands rather than a scheduled ferry, it carries no vehicles, and berths sell out weeks ahead. Similarly named Colombia-to-Panama boat trips such as San Blas Adventures actually start from Capurgana and Sapzurro, not Cartagena, and no scheduled passenger or vehicle ferry currently links Cartagena with Panama.

half.name: Islas del Rosario
half.blurb: A coral archipelago an hour offshore with turquoise water, snorkeling and beach-club day passes.

half.name: Playa Blanca (Barú)
half.blurb: The white-sand, palm-lined beach on the Barú peninsula, reachable by boat or road.

half.name: Volcán del Totumo
half.blurb: A small mud volcano north of the city where visitors bathe in warm mineral mud.

half.name: La Boquilla
half.blurb: A fishing village of mangrove canoe tours and beachfront seafood shacks just north of Cartagena.

full.name: Santa Marta
full.blurb: Colombia's oldest city and gateway to Tayrona National Park's jungle-backed Caribbean beaches (~4h).

full.name: Mompox
full.blurb: A time-capsule colonial river town on the Magdalena, famous for filigree silver (a long day or overnight).

full.name: Barranquilla
full.blurb: Colombia's Caribbean industrial capital, home of the country's biggest Carnival (~2h).
